problem: The sentence "If θ  φ, it slides unless P is applied" has lost its comparison sign, so the key condition is unreadable and a student cannot tell whether it means θ > φ or θ < φ.
fix: If θ > φ, the block slides down unless a force P is applied. Equivalently, the block stays by itself only when θ ≤ φ, that is μ ≥ tan θ.

where: Section 2, start of the P derivation
problem: The equilibrium P + f = W sin θ only holds when P acts up the plane, but this direction is never stated, so the minus sign in P_min looks arbitrary.
fix: Take P as a force applied parallel to the plane and directed up the slope. Then for impending motion down the plane, P + f = W sin θ.

where: Section 2 and Section 3, the P_min ≤ P ≤ P_max statement
problem: When θ < φ (that is μ > tan θ), P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ comes out negative. The claim "any P between P_min and P_max keeps the block in equilibrium" then suggests a negative force, which confuses students.
fix: Add: if θ ≤ φ, then P_min ≤ 0 and the block stands on its own; the safe range is then 0 ≤ P ≤ P_max, and P_min only tells the downward force needed to start sliding down. Use P_min = W sin θ − μW cos θ only when θ > φ.

problem: The symbol φ appears in "Hence φ = tan⁻¹ μ" without being named as the angle of repose in that sentence.
fix: Write: Hence the angle of repose is φ = tan⁻¹ μ, where φ is measured from the horizontal.

problem: "The normal reaction is smaller than the weight because the slope tilts the block away from vertical" is vague; the real reason is that N is only the component of W perpendicular to the plane.
fix: The normal reaction is smaller than the weight because only the perpendicular component W cos θ of the weight presses on the plane; the rest, W sin θ, acts along the plane.
